title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples

epigraph.quote: The best way to predict the future is to design the supply chain that delivers it.
epigraph.author: Anonymous

web_blocks.html: Lenskart Solutions Ltd. is a vertically integrated eyewear retailer. It designs, manufactures, brands, and sells prescription glasses, sunglasses, and contact lenses across 3,300+ global stores [1][2][3]. Roughly 59% of revenue comes from India (>2,600 stores) and 41% from international markets (Owndays and Meller) [6][9][12]. Lenskart runs a 'house of brands' spanning Vincent Chase, John Jacobs, Lenskart Air, Aqualens, Owndays, and Meller [2][6][9].

web_blocks.takeaway: Lenskart is overwhelmingly a medical-necessity prescription eyewear business (>80% of product revenue) with a 59%/41% India-to-International split, insulated from pure discretionary fashion volatility while using sunglasses and contact lenses as low-CAC acquisition funnels.

web_blocks.html: To see how the business earns each rupee, trace a real customer journey in each segment.

web_blocks.title: Concrete Real-World Example 1: Prescription Eyeglasses (Tier-2 India Omnichannel Order)
paragraphs: A software engineer in Indore notices eye strain and downloads the Lenskart app. She books a ₹99 'Home Eye Test' or visits a nearby Lenskart store for a 12-step robotic eye exam. She picks two Vincent Chase frames using Lenskart Gold (Buy-One-Get-One) for roughly ₹3,500–₹4,500.

The store tablet sends her prescription straight to Bhiwadi's automated lens lab. Robotics grind, coat, and edge the lenses, shipping finished glasses within 24 to 72 hours [8]. Her prescription stays in the cloud, turning an 18-to-24-month replacement into a frictionless reorder.

web_blocks.title: Concrete Real-World Example 2: Sunglasses & Fashion Adjacency (Meller & John Jacobs)
paragraphs: A college student in Bengaluru sees an Instagram ad for Meller—the Barcelona sunglasses brand Lenskart acquired in July 2025 [9]. She buys a ₹2,800 polarized pair online or at a mall kiosk. Private-label sourcing yields ~65%–70% gross margins while expanding Lenskart's fashion reach.

web_blocks.title: Concrete Real-World Example 3: Contact Lenses & Recurring Replenishment (Aqualens)
paragraphs: A Mumbai consultant wears monthly disposable lenses for the gym and weekends. He subscribes to Lenskart's private-label Aqualens packs at ₹1,200–₹1,800 per box instead of costlier imported brands. Monthly and quarterly reorders keep customers active on the Lenskart app year-round.

web_blocks.title: Concrete Real-World Example 4: International Operations (Owndays Japan & SE Asia)
paragraphs: In Tokyo or Singapore, a commuter walks into an Owndays store inside a rail mall [6]. Owndays offers a flat all-inclusive price (frame plus standard index lenses) with 20-minute on-site lens cutting. Lenskart is migrating Owndays' backend sourcing to India to lift international margins toward India levels.

web_blocks.html: Across all four segments, Gold membership drives 35%–37% repeat orders at minimal acquisition cost [10]. Over 80% of revenue comes from recurring prescription eyewear, insulating the business from pure fashion cycles.

Why does this product mix matter for revenue durability? Prescription eyewear (>80% of sales) behaves like a non-discretionary medical staple rather than pure fashion [2]. Customers replace glasses every 18 to 24 months as eye power shifts or frames wear out. Sunglasses (10%–15%) add higher-margin fashion upside through Vincent Chase, John Jacobs, and Meller [2][9]. Aqualens contact lenses (5%–10%) turn an infrequent purchase into monthly or quarterly app reorders. Geographically, India (~59% of sales) delivers higher store margins, while Owndays (~41% of sales) provides scale across 13 Asian markets [6][12].

Store economics also benefit from a wide price ladder across segments [2][11]. Entry-level Vincent Chase prescription glasses start near ₹1,500–₹2,500, drawing first-time buyers out of unorganized shops. Mid-tier John Jacobs and Lenskart Air frames lift average selling prices to ₹3,500–₹5,500 in metros. Meanwhile, Owndays and Meller capture higher-ticket international and fashion demand [6][9]. That multi-brand ladder lets Lenskart serve both Tier-3 towns and Tokyo commuter malls without diluting its core brand.

book_paragraphs: To really understand Lenskart, you have to stop thinking of it as an e-commerce website and start seeing it as an industrial healthcare-retail machine. When you walk past a Lenskart storefront in a mall in Pune, a high street in Jaipur, or a subway concourse in Tokyo under the Owndays banner, you are looking at the front end of a single, unified business: designing, manufacturing, testing, and dispensing prescription eyewear.

More than 80% of Lenskart's core product revenue comes from prescription eyeglasses—frames fitted with custom-ground lenses for nearsightedness, farsightedness, astigmatism, or progressive presbyopia. That single statistic is the bedrock of the business's resilience. Unlike sneakers or handbags, you cannot postpone buying prescription glasses indefinitely when your eyesight blurs or your frame snaps. Sunglasses account for another 10% to 15% of the product mix—bolstered by the 2025 acquisition of Barcelona-based Meller—while contact lenses and solutions under the Aqualens label contribute roughly 5% to 10%.

Geographically, Lenskart has evolved into a two-engine enterprise. India generates roughly 59% of consolidated FY26 revenue of ₹8,814 crore and remains the primary profit and growth engine, expanding around 35% year-on-year as stores push deeper into Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities. International operations—anchored by Owndays across Japan and 12 Asian markets, alongside stores in the Middle East and Meller in Europe—contribute the remaining 41%.

Looking across all three product lines—prescription eyewear (>80%), sunglasses (10%–15%), and Aqualens contact lenses (5%–10%)—plus the 59% India and 41% International geographic split, you can see why Lenskart behaves like an ecosystem rather than a single-product retailer. Prescription glasses bring high-margin clinical traffic into stores; Gold memberships lock in repeat households; contact lenses create high-frequency digital reorders; and sunglasses capture younger fashion-led buyers. Few consumer businesses in India have built such a tightly interlocking product flywheel.

book_subsections.title: Four Customers, One Integrated Back-End
paragraphs: Let's walk through what those segments look like on the ground. Picture a young professional in Indore who books a Lenskart Home Eye Test on her phone. An optometrist arrives at her living room with a portable autorefractor, tests her vision, lets her try on physical sample frames, and uploads her prescription on a tablet. Within minutes, that digital order hits Lenskart's automated facility in Bhiwadi, where robotic arms pick the Vincent Chase frame, grind and coat the polycarbonate lenses, verify the optical power with automated scanners, and ship the finished glasses to her door within days. Because Lenskart owns the brand and the factory, it keeps roughly 70% gross margins while charging half what a legacy optician charges for imported frames.

Now picture three other customers feeding the exact same machine. A college student in Bengaluru sees an Instagram reel for Meller, walks into one of 500 Lenskart stores carrying the European brand, and buys a pair of polarized sunglasses off the shelf with zero lab wait time. A consultant in Mumbai subscribes to Aqualens contact lenses on the app, reordering every quarter and keeping Lenskart top-of-mind between spectacle purchases. And a commuter in Tokyo steps into an Owndays store in a train station, picks a frame at a transparent all-in price, and walks out with finished single-vision glasses in twenty minutes—increasingly supplied by Lenskart's lower-cost Asian manufacturing network.

book_subsections.title: Walking the Store Floor: Product Mix, Geography & Unit Realities
paragraphs: Let's break down what Lenskart actually sells inside those 3,300+ global stores. Prescription eyeglasses are the undisputed anchor, generating over 80% of consolidated revenue. Unlike discretionary sunglasses, prescription eyewear is a medical necessity with built-in replacement cycles every 18 to 24 months as prescriptions shift or frames wear out. Sunglasses account for roughly 10% to 15% of revenue, boosted by fashion-forward labels like Vincent Chase, John Jacobs, and newly acquired Meller, while contact lenses under the Aqualens brand contribute the remaining 5% to 10% with high-frequency monthly and quarterly repeat orders.

Geographically, the business is roughly 59% India and 41% International. India remains the high-growth profitability engine: Lenskart operates over 2,600 stores across metros and Tier-2/3 cities, adding 542 net new Indian stores in FY26 alone while delivering 14.3% pre-Ind AS EBITDA margins and 20% to 28% same-store sales growth. International operations—anchored by Owndays across Japan and Southeast Asia plus emerging hubs in the Middle East and Europe—added 61 net new stores in FY26 and operate at a leaner 7.0% pre-Ind AS EBITDA margin due to higher developed-market store rents and optometrist wages.

Think about how these segments reinforce each other through the Gold Membership program. A customer who walks into a Pune or Bengaluru store for a free 12-step robotic eye test pays ₹500 to ₹800 for a Gold membership, receives a Buy-One-Get-One pair of Vincent Chase frames with anti-glare lenses, and returns six months later via the app to reorder Aqualens contacts or a spare pair of sunglasses. Over 35% to 37% of sales come from repeat Gold members at virtually zero incremental customer acquisition cost.

book_subsections.title: The Corporate & Tier-2 Customer Reality: Two Concrete Walkthroughs
paragraphs: Consider two everyday customers who illustrate why Lenskart's model travels so well across income tiers. First, picture a 29-year-old software engineer in Bengaluru who spends ten hours a day in front of dual monitors. She books a free home eye test or steps into an Indiranagar Lenskart store, undergoes a 12-step robotic refraction check, and buys two pairs of John Jacobs blue-light-blocking prescription glasses for roughly ₹4,500 using her Gold membership. Her prescription and pupillary distance are saved in the cloud; eighteen months later, she reorders a fresh pair or Aqualens daily disposables in three taps on her phone.

Now picture a first-time spectacle buyer in a Tier-2 city like Jaipur or Indore. Historically, he faced a stark choice: pay ₹8,000+ at an upscale boutique or gamble on inconsistent quality at a neighborhood optician. At a Lenskart franchise store, he gets a standardized digital eye test, browses 1,000+ Vincent Chase frames priced transparently at ₹1,500 to ₹2,500 with anti-glare lenses included, and walks away with a 1-year warranty. That combination of clinical standardization and transparent pricing is what unlocks 20% to 28% same-store sales growth in India.

book_subsections.title: Why Contact Lenses and Sunglasses Matter More Than Their Share
paragraphs: While prescription glasses drive over 80% of revenue, sunglasses (10%–15%) and Aqualens contact lenses (5%–10%) play a strategic role that goes beyond their current top-line slice. Contact lenses turn an 18-to-24-month replacement cycle into a monthly or quarterly habit, keeping the Lenskart app on the customer's home screen and driving recurring cross-sell at near-zero acquisition cost.

Meanwhile, the July 2025 acquisition of an 80% stake in European D2C brand Meller for roughly ₹407 Cr gives Lenskart a fast-fashion sunglasses engine capable of capturing younger urban shoppers across both Europe and India.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: Why Prescription Beats Pure Fashion
book_callouts.text: If Lenskart were selling only sunglasses, you and I would worry constantly about fashion cycles, discounting, and fickle consumer tastes. Because over 80% of its revenue is anchored in prescription eyewear—and backed by automated optometry and a 9-million-member Gold loyalty loop—the business behaves far more like recurring healthcare retail than discretionary apparel. Yet notice the trade-off: international revenue is 41% of the pie today, and Owndays operates at roughly half the pre-Ind AS EBITDA margin of India. In Chapter 3, we will dissect the unit economics to see how much of every ₹100 in sales actually survives to cash flow.
